1321.event_title: Nizami tells how Khosrow pleads at the gate of Shirin's castle
1321.event: The Persian poet Nizami of Ganja wrote the romance Khosrow and Shirin, later counted among the five poems of his Khamsa, about the Sasanian king Khosrow Parviz and the Armenian princess Shirin. In one of its most famous episodes Shirin, displeased with Khosrow's behaviour and his marriage to another woman, withdraws to her castle. After his queen's death Khosrow comes again and again to see her, standing at her gate at dawn in the depth of winter, until Shirin finally yields and the lovers are reconciled.
1321.explanation: The scene became one of the most painted subjects in Persian art, a classic image of a beloved's withdrawal drawing out a lover's humble and devoted pleading.
1321.tie_back: This kural says a little sulking has the power to draw out more of a lover's tenderness, and Shirin's retreat to her castle draws from King Khosrow the most devoted pleading of the whole romance.
1321._accuracy_note: The withdrawal-then-greater-tenderness pattern fits well, but in the poem Khosrow is not blameless, whereas the kural stresses that the beloved sulks even when there is no fault.

1322.event_title: Tennyson and Emily Sellwood marry after ten years apart
1322.event: Alfred Tennyson fell in love with Emily Sellwood in 1836 and the two came to consider themselves engaged, but in 1840 all relations between them were broken off. In 1849 Tennyson resumed his correspondence with Emily, and in June 1850, less than two weeks after the publication of his poem In Memoriam, they were quietly married at Shiplake Church. Their marriage, which lasted until his death, is described as happy and full of tenderness and affection.
1322.explanation: It is a well-documented case of a love that seemed to have withered for a decade and then returned to become a lifelong marriage.
1322.tie_back: The kural says that love may droop for a while and then return with greater glory, which is what happened when Tennyson and Emily Sellwood came back together after ten years apart.
1322._accuracy_note: The droop-and-revival of love matches closely, but the long break was not a playful lovers' sulk, and sources disagree on exactly why the engagement was broken off.

1323.event_title: A. K. Ramanujan publishes The Interior Landscape
1323.event: In 1967 the poet and scholar A. K. Ramanujan, then teaching at the University of Chicago, published The Interior Landscape: Love Poems from a Classical Tamil Anthology. The book brought classical Tamil love poetry to English readers in clear, modern translations. Ramanujan went on to translate many more classical Tamil poems and was honoured by the government of India with the Padma Shri in 1976.
1323.explanation: The Interior Landscape made the ancient Tamil poetry of love, with its famous images of lovers whose hearts mingle, known to readers far beyond India.
1323.tie_back: This kural compares lovers to water blended with earth, an image rooted in the classical Tamil love poetry that Ramanujan's book introduced to the wider world.
1323._accuracy_note: The book connects directly to the Tamil love-poetry tradition behind the kural's simile, but it is a publishing event rather than a real couple whose quarrel was sweeter than heaven.

1324.event_title: Johnny Cash proposes to June Carter on stage
1324.event: During a concert at the London Gardens arena in London, Ontario, on 22 February 1968, Johnny Cash proposed marriage to June Carter on stage in front of about 7,000 people. Cash had proposed to her on stage many times before, and this time she said yes. The two were married on 1 March 1968.
1324.explanation: The moment became one of the most famous proposals in music history and is now marked by a public mural in London, Ontario.
1324.tie_back: The kural speaks of a weapon hidden in the lover's pleading that breaks down the beloved's resolve, and Cash's repeated proposals finally overcame June Carter's long reluctance.
1324._accuracy_note: It shows persistent pleading breaking down a beloved's resistance, though June Carter's earlier refusals were not a lovers' sulk within a marriage.

1325.event_title: Georgia O'Keeffe spends her first summer in New Mexico
1325.event: In the summer of 1929 the painter Georgia O'Keeffe left New York and her husband, the photographer Alfred Stieglitz, to spend time in northern New Mexico, staying first in Taos. Her letters from there were full of happiness, while Stieglitz wrote that he was broken by her absence. For the next two decades she spent most summers working in New Mexico, and their marriage, sustained by thousands of letters, lasted until Stieglitz died in 1946.
1325.explanation: The O'Keeffe and Stieglitz letters are a well-known record of a couple who found that time apart could renew both their work and their bond.
1325.tie_back: The kural says that being kept apart for a while from one's beloved, even without fault, holds a pleasure of its own, and O'Keeffe's summers away brought her joy without ending her marriage.
1325._accuracy_note: The separation was a real source of happiness for O'Keeffe, but it caused Stieglitz pain, so the event only partly matches the kural's sweet, temporary parting.

1326.event_title: Much Ado About Nothing, with its quarrelling lovers, is published
1326.event: William Shakespeare's comedy Much Ado About Nothing was first published in 1600. In it Beatrice and Benedick keep up a running battle of wit and insults, kept apart by pride and mutual antagonism, until their friends trick each of them into believing the other is secretly in love. Even at the end they carry on teasing each other, but when love poems in their own handwriting are produced, they agree to marry.
1326.explanation: Beatrice and Benedick became the model for countless later stories in which lovers' quarrelling turns out to be the very spice of their love.
1326.tie_back: This kural says that in love the quarrel is sweeter than the union, and Shakespeare's pair show how sparring can make love livelier than calm agreement.
1326._accuracy_note: The play captures the kural's delight in lovers' quarrelling, though Beatrice and Benedick spar before marriage rather than sulk within it.

1327.event_title: The Marriage of Figaro premieres in Vienna
1327.event: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's comic opera The Marriage of Figaro, with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte, premiered at the Burgtheater in Vienna on 1 May 1786. In the story the jealous Count Almaviva, caught out after suspecting his wife, is forced to beg the Countess's forgiveness, and at the opera's conclusion he again asks for her pardon. Britannica describes the work as a tale of love, betrayal and forgiveness.
1327.explanation: The forgiveness scene is one of the most celebrated moments in opera, showing a proud nobleman who wins back peace only by humbling himself.
1327.tie_back: The kural says the one who loses in a lovers' quarrel is the real winner, and in Figaro the Count gains reconciliation only when he gives way and asks forgiveness.
1327._accuracy_note: The opera dramatises winning through yielding, but it is a fictional story and the Count's faults are real, unlike the gentle lovers' sulk of the kural.

1328.event_title: A Mewar artist paints Radha Awaiting Reconciliation with Krishna
1328.event: About 1680 an artist of the Rajput kingdom of Mewar painted a page for a Gita Govinda manuscript, now in the Cleveland Museum of Art, titled Radha Awaiting Reconciliation with Krishna. The painting shows Radha six times as she prepares flowering bowers for their meeting and pleads with a picture of Krishna, while her confidante appeals to him. Such paintings belonged to a wider tradition of Rajasthani miniatures in the 17th and 18th centuries inspired by Jayadeva's poem of estrangement and reunion.
1328.explanation: The painting shows how Indian artists turned the longing for a lovers' reconciliation into an image meant to be felt by the viewer.
1328.tie_back: The kural wonders whether, through a little sulking, the lovers can once more win the sweetness of reunion they knew before, which is exactly the hope Radha acts out in this painting.
1328._accuracy_note: The painting captures the longing for a renewed reunion, but it depicts a mythological scene, and only the museum record documents this particular work.

1329.event_title: Antoine Galland publishes The Thousand and One Nights in French
1329.event: Between 1704 and 1717 the French scholar Antoine Galland published Les Mille et Une Nuits in twelve volumes, the first European translation of The Thousand and One Nights. In its frame story Shahrazad tells the king a story each evening, leaving it unfinished so that he wishes to hear the end, until he finally abandons his cruel plan. Galland's version caused a craze across Europe and was itself translated into many languages.
1329.explanation: Galland's work brought one of the world's great story collections to the West and made Shahrazad's night-after-night storytelling famous.
1329.tie_back: The lover in this kural wishes the night would grow longer so that he can go on pleading, and the most famous story of a speaker who stretches out the nights with her words is Shahrazad's.
1329._accuracy_note: The theme of lengthened nights filled with persuasive words carries over, but Shahrazad is saving lives, not coaxing a sulking beloved.

1330.event: In the 12th century the poet Jayadeva, at the court of King Lakshmanasena of Bengal, composed the Sanskrit song-poem Gitagovinda in twelve cantos. It tells how Radha, seeing Krishna with other cowherd girls, becomes jealous, rebukes him when he comes to her, and slowly softens as he pleads with her, until the lovers are joyfully united. The poem spread across India, inspired many paintings, and is still sung at the Jagannatha temple in Puri.
1330.explanation: The Gitagovinda is one of the best-known works of Indian literature to treat a lovers' quarrel and reconciliation as the very heart of love.
1330.tie_back: This last kural says sulking is the delight of love and the delight of sulking is to be held close again, the exact path from jealousy to joyful reunion that the Gitagovinda traces.
1330._accuracy_note: The poem's arc from sulk to embrace closely mirrors the kural, though it is a devotional poem about divine lovers rather than a historical couple.
